# task-f3b849f1: horizontal pivot-aligned template stamping

## New recurrence (26x29, unresolved; eight wrong submissions)

Current test: background 7 with many isolated color-0 pixels. A 3-cell vertical object at column 14, rows 7-9 is `[6,1,4]`; there is also an isolated 0 at (8,28). Eight demos were requested and all eight were heterogeneous, so no single precise rule was established. Six prior submissions were rejected before the attempt cap, covering guesses that (a) copy local 3x3/cross motifs from the 6/1/4 object, (b) spread values 1, 6, or 0 on aligned marker locations, and (c) leave the field unchanged. None should be reused as a validated solution. Exact eighth prediction is recorded in session, not validated.

Demos from this instance:
1) 23x8 bg4; sparse 3 anchors and horizontal seed `[8,8,6,6,8]` at r11 c3-7. Each 3 is replaced by a horizontal copy of this sequence, pivot-aligned on the marker at seed offset 2 (copy starts at anchor-2).
2) 29x19 bg8; sparse 4 anchors and seed `[1,9,3,9,9]` at r11 c13-17. Copies are placed horizontally centered/pivoted on anchors; behavior includes clipping at edges.
3) 13x10 bg4; source horizontal 3-cell pattern `[7,8,5]` in rows 3-4, cols1-3, pivot 8 at offset 1; sparse 3 anchors receive that motif with pivot aligned, both horizontal and vertical placements observed (vertical source/replication context differs).
4) 29x16 bg1; 3x3-ish source motif near top left, sparse 6 anchors; output copies motif horizontally at anchor-aligned location and also vertically around a lower anchor, indicating heterogeneous behavior.
5) 12x23 bg2; seed `[8,1,8]` at bottom row c9-11, sparse 4s. Each 4 is replaced by this motif with center 1 aligned to trigger; horizontal only.
6) 20x23 bg3; source is composite 5x3 multicolor motif at r0-4 c5-7, sparse 9s receive motif stamps with alignment/rotation-like offsets; preserve bg and source.
7) 29x27 bg5; horizontal motif `[6,8,8,6,8]` at r15 c21-25, sparse 4s act as anchors; stamps align pivot (first 6) to marker, horizontal.
8) 10x20 bg2; seed `[7,7,5,8,0]` at r8 c11-15, sparse 3 markers; stamps align anchor to offset 2 (5) and replace anchor with 5.

These examples strongly support a recurring family of marker-aligned motif copying, but not one universal orientation/pivot/seed-selection rule. In this test, all motifs are isolated 0 markers, while the only multicolor pattern is a vertical line [6,1,4] at r7-9,c14; demos do not show whether that line is a seed, whether every 0 is an anchor, what pivot is, or whether stamps go horizontally/vertically. Importantly, previous trial submissions included output grids that incorrectly placed several unrelated transformations; all were rejected. Preserve unresolved status; do not treat task ID or generic copy motif as sufficient.

Accepted test was 14x16, background 0. Seed is the 3×3 motif at rows 10–12, cols 0–2:
`[[1,2,2],[9,1,9],[0,0,3]]`. Eight isolated color-6 cells are at (2,1),(2,5),(3,12),(6,3),(7,10),(9,14),(11,10),(12,5) (zero-based). For each isolated 6, stamp the seed motif with its central cell (seed value 1) aligned to that trigger coordinate. Thus each motif occupies trigger row±1, col±1, clipped to grid boundaries. Preserve seed and all other cells; where stamps overlap, stamp values agree on this test. This exact rule was accepted after 5 wrong submissions (some invalid-grid serialization); output is 14×16.

Consequently, apply this rule only when the current input has a clear horizontal multicolor seed with a pivot matching the sparse trigger arrangement and current demos support same-row copies. ## Validation
Extract seed values and pivot index from the current input; do not assume these literal colors or length recur. # Heterogeneous Continual-ARC demo triage

## Use when
A recurring task ID has a history of unresolved instances, or current demonstrations alter localized objects in ways that vary across palette, position, size, and context. Do not assume the shared task ID or broad visual family defines a reusable transformation.

## Procedure
1. Inventory each demo's dimensions, palette, objects, and exact input-output deltas. Track unchanged objects that resemble the changed object; they often constrain the trigger.
2. Compare demos on candidate selection features: object shape/area, position, boundary contact, adjacency, multiplicity, and relation to other components. Keep a rule only if it explains all changed and unchanged cases.
3. Compare the test against the demos structurally. A broadly similar theme (such as isolated colored shapes) is not sufficient if the distinguishing geometry/context is absent.
4. Request another demo when it can separate explicit competing hypotheses. Consider the stated demo and wrong-attempt costs; don't ask indiscriminately, but don't submit unsupported variants just to try a color or region.
5. Submit only when one complete rule predicts the entire output. If unresolved, continue with an informative demo rather than no-op, repeated recoloring, or cosmetic variants. After rejection, discard the tested rule and reassess.
6. Validate output dimensions, row lengths, coordinates, and palette. In Continual-ARC, return exactly one JSON action object and no prose.

## Pitfalls
- Task-ID recurrence is not proof that examples share a simple rule; evidence may remain unresolved across many instances.
- Localized edits in demos do not establish global color mappings or which test object should change.
- No-op outputs and near-identical guesses are not useful exploration; use demonstrations to resolve uncertainty.
- Do not present an untested hypothesis as a reliable procedure.

# Continual-ARC demo budget and triage

## Workflow
1. After every input-output pair, summarize its actual transformation and compare exact changed and unchanged cells; do not infer a shared rule from broad visual similarity or task ID.
2. Before requesting a demo, state the unresolved property, why resolving it could change the test output, and what structural features a useful demo must share with the test. Prefer a request that distinguishes explicit competing hypotheses.
3. Assess each returned example against that question. If it is structurally unrelated and leaves the ambiguity unchanged, count it as no useful evidence; repeated generic requests are not progress.
4. Stop requesting when the remaining demo is unlikely to discriminate the test-relevant hypotheses. If no coherent rule explains the demos and predicts the test, retain uncertainty rather than making an unsupported submission.
5. A wrong submission falsifies the complete prediction tested. Reset and reassess; never spend attempts on cosmetic palette, direction, or subset variants absent new evidence.
6. Preserve the interface contract: exactly one action JSON object per turn, and mechanically validate output dimensions, row lengths, and palette before submitting.

## Pitfalls
- Heterogeneous demonstrations can reflect different mechanisms despite sharing a task identifier or sparse-marker appearance.
- A long sequence of unrelated demos does not increase confidence in an untested hypothesis.
- Motif presence alone does not establish template, pivot, target eligibility, orientation, or placement constraints; each is part of the rule.
